# ChatGPT and Teens: What Parents Actually Need to Know

> **In short:** ChatGPT's terms of service set a minimum age, and OpenAI has discussed extra safeguards for younger users — but the specific protections, what they cover, and how parent controls work aren't something we can confirm in detail. Here's how to think through the question for your own family.

Your 14-year-old just asked if they can use ChatGPT for homework help. Maybe you've heard mixed things — too much screen time, accuracy worries, content concerns. Before you say yes, no, or "ask me later," it helps to know what's actually in your control and what isn't.

## The age question, first

ChatGPT's official terms set a minimum age — 13 in most regions, and higher in some places. Anyone younger isn't supposed to have an account. That's the legal floor, and your household rules can absolutely be stricter. If your child is under the minimum, the answer is simply "not yet," regardless of what a friend at school is doing.

For older teens, the question shifts from "is it allowed" to "is it a good idea in our family."

## What ChatGPT does well — and badly

Worth knowing before any conversation with your kid:

- It's good at explaining concepts, summarizing long texts, and brainstorming ideas.
- It confidently makes things up — wrong dates, fake citations, invented quotes. Anything that matters (a grade, a paper, a fact in an argument) should be double-checked elsewhere.
- It can still produce content that isn't appropriate for younger users, even with built-in filters. No filter is perfect.
- It doesn't replace real conversation. For mental health, friendships, or tough decisions, it should never be the only voice in the room.

## What you can and can't control

This is the part parents most often ask about, and honesty matters here:

- **Account-level controls are limited.** ChatGPT does not currently offer the kind of detailed parent dashboard some other apps do. You can't see every prompt your teen types from your own phone.
- **Family conversations matter more than settings.** Agreeing on what it's for — homework, not emotional advice — and when it's off-limits (late at night, during meals) tends to work better than any technical lock.
- **OpenAI has talked about stronger protections for younger users.** Whether those are rolled out, what they include, and how parents opt in is something to check directly on OpenAI's site before assuming they're available.

## What this means for you

- **If you're a parent of a teen (roughly 13–17)**: Treat ChatGPT like any other tool with real upsides and real risks. The most useful thing you can do is stay curious about how your teen is using it, rather than ban it or ignore it.
- **If you're a parent of a younger child**: The minimum age isn't a suggestion. When the time comes, kid-focused AI tools built for younger children will be a better fit.
- **If you're a teen reading this**: Use it for what it's actually good at — homework explanations, brainstorming, learning new things. Tell a real person if it ever says something that bothers you.
- **If you're an educator or librarian**: Worth introducing students to both the capabilities and the limits, including the habit of double-checking facts.

## Wrap-up

The honest answer is that no tool replaces your judgment as the adult in the room. The next step that helps most families: spend ten minutes with your teen asking what they'd actually use ChatGPT for, and decide together what your house rules will be. That conversation matters more than any setting.
